problem-list.title: Problem list implementation
problem-list.subtitle: Implementing a structured SNOMED CT-based problem list in clinical systems
problem-list.overview: A SNOMED CT-based problem list enables structured condition recording that supports longitudinal care, clinical decision support, cohort queries, and interoperability. Concepts from the Clinical finding and Disorder hierarchies are used, scoped by an Expression Constraint Language (ECL) expression or a curated reference set. This is one of the highest-value and most common SNOMED CT implementation targets.

decisions.question: What constitutes a 'problem' in your clinical context?
decisions.guidance: There is no single definition of a 'problem' - it varies by specialty, care setting, and organisation. Clarify whether the list covers active conditions only, includes resolved history, or captures the full range of health concerns. Treat this as a critical starting point, not a detail to settle later: it determines which SNOMED CT hierarchies and value set bindings the rest of the implementation is built on. This is a clinical governance decision - scope agreed early is hard to reverse once data is being captured.

decisions.question: Will concept selection be open or constrained by a value set?
decisions.guidance: An open and high-level constraint (any descendant of Clinical finding) gives maximum flexibility and granularity, but searching across thousands of concepts demands an efficient search mechanism. Relevance ranking, frequency-based ordering, or context-aware suggestions become essential as the constraint gets broader. A manually curated subset is quick to define and easy for clinicians to accept, but it lacks the granularity of a hierarchical (ECL-bounded) constraint and needs more maintenance as SNOMED CT content evolves. A managed subset is often an easy starting point for this reason, widening over time - or giving way to an ECL-bounded constraint. See the Value Sets playbook for how to define and govern it.

decisions.question: What level of clinical granularity is required?
decisions.guidance: The right granularity is rarely a single choice across a workflow: CDS rules and patient-level analytics need the most specific concept the clinician can confidently assert, while population-level reporting can aggregate upward using subsumption (<<) rather than forcing coarser data entry. Capture at the most specific level available and aggregate for reporting, rather than constraining entry to a coarser grain up front. Agree the required depth with clinicians and informaticists before building search and validation logic.

decisions.question: How will preferred terms be displayed to clinicians?
decisions.guidance: SNOMED CT fully specified names (FSNs) is not intended for direct data entry and display in the clinical user interface. Preferred terms from the appropriate language reference set should be the default display term for data entry. If your system is multilingual, agree on the language priority order.

decisions.question: What is the architecture of the implementation and how is the problem list integrated into the clinical system?
decisions.guidance: Understand the technical architecture before making value set and terminology service decisions. Key questions: Is the problem list a module within an existing EHR, or a standalone system? Can a FHIR terminology service be integrated directly, or must value sets be loaded statically? Is the system built in-house or a commercial product with constraints on integration? The answers determine which value set delivery approach is feasible and how much of the SNOMED CT infrastructure the implementation team controls.

decisions.question: How will the problem list feed downstream systems?
decisions.guidance: Identify which systems consume problem list data - CDS engines, analytics platforms, ICD-10 reporting, FHIR document exchange. Each has different requirements that will constrain your SNOMED CT implementation choices.

steps.title: Define clinical scope and governance policy
steps.description: Work with clinical and governance leads to agree what constitutes a 'problem', who approves changes to the scope, and how the list will be maintained over time.

steps.title: Define the problem list value set
steps.description: Define the concept scope using an ECL expression (e.g. <<404684003 for all clinical findings, or a narrower constraint) or a curated subset. ECL is preferred - it automatically includes new concepts added in each SNOMED CT release. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and testing guidance.

examples.label: ECL for clinical findings
examples.code:
# All clinical findings (broadest scope)
<<404684003 |Clinical finding (finding)|

# Disorders only (common for problem lists)
<<64572001 |Disease (disorder)|

# Exclude administrative concepts
<<404684003 MINUS <<413350009 |Finding with explicit context|

steps.title: Choose how the value set will be delivered
steps.description: Decide whether a FHIR terminology service will be integrated directly into the clinical system (best practice) or whether the value set will be exported as a static concept list. Direct integration keeps concept and term data current with each SNOMED CT release; static exports must be refreshed manually. See the Value set playbook for delivery patterns and trade-offs.

steps.title: Package the value set for the clinical system
steps.description: A raw list of concept IDs is not sufficient - the clinical system needs terms and a structured format. With an integrated terminology service, define a FHIR ValueSet with an ECL compose expression; preferred terms are resolved at runtime. Without one, export the expanded concept list with preferred terms and package as a FHIR ValueSet, RF2 reference set, or CSV. Static representations must be refreshed on each SNOMED CT release. See the Value set playbook for packaging options.

steps.title: Implement clinician-facing search
steps.description: Configure search to display preferred terms from the language reference set - never FSNs. Apply the ECL constraint as a search filter on the terminology service API. Default ranking rarely surfaces the most clinically relevant result first - frequency-based and preferred-term boosting need to be layered on top. See the Search and data entry playbook for ranking, synonym configuration, and no-match handling.

steps.title: Establish governance and release management
steps.description: Define who reviews the value set on each SNOMED CT release, how inactivated concepts are handled in existing patient data, and how clinicians can request new concepts or additions to the value set.

dependencies.text: SNOMED CT terminology service - either integrated into the clinical system (best practice) or used separately to extract and export value sets
ECL-defined clinical finding value set or reference set
Clinical and terminology governance framework
Language reference set configured for preferred term display

pitfalls: Displaying FSNs (fully specified names) instead of preferred terms from a language reference set - FSNs are not for clinical display
Using an open constraint (all of SNOMED CT) without scoping - this produces irrelevant search results and poor data quality
Failing to configure the correct national edition in the terminology service, causing local concepts to be missing
Skipping release management - inactivated concepts silently remain in patient records after SNOMED CT updates
Using a static value set extracted from a terminology server without a refresh process - new clinically relevant concepts added in SNOMED CT releases are silently excluded from selection

clin-docs.title: Structured clinical documentation
clin-docs.subtitle: Capturing structured clinical data using SNOMED CT in templates and forms
clin-docs.overview: Structured clinical documentation using SNOMED CT supplements - and sometimes replaces - free text with computable, queryable data. Data entry fields are bound to SNOMED CT value sets, giving clinicians access to clinically appropriate concepts at the point of care. SNOMED International and national release centres publish domain-specific implementation guides that define patterns for recording specific types of clinical information, such as allergies and adverse reactions. The key challenge is balancing clinical expressiveness with usability: over-structuring creates friction, while under-structuring produces data that cannot be queried or exchanged.

decisions.question: Which clinical data elements need to be SNOMED CT coded, and which can remain as narrative?
decisions.guidance: Not every field should be coded. Focus SNOMED CT binding on data that will be queried, exchanged, or used for decision support. Mandatory structured fields with poor UX lead to workarounds - start with the highest-value fields and expand progressively.

decisions.question: How will clinical meaning and context be represented for each structured element?
decisions.guidance: Consider not just what value to capture, but what it means in context. A finding field may need to distinguish between a confirmed finding, a suspected finding, a family history, or an excluded condition. The Context Representation Implementation Guide defines patterns for capturing such meaning. These decisions affect template design, value set scope, and what downstream queries can reliably answer.

decisions.question: What are the value set binding principles for each structured field?
decisions.guidance: Value set binding defines the permissible SNOMED CT concepts for a field. Approaches include ECL-based hierarchy constraints, curated reference sets, and combinations. ECL is a powerful tool for hierarchy-based constraints but not the only approach - some fields are better served by curated lists or reference sets where clinical judgement over individual concepts is required. The binding approach should match the clinical purpose and be maintainable over time. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and governance guidance.

decisions.question: Are there logic rules or dependencies between data elements that need to be established?
decisions.guidance: Some documentation fields are clinically interdependent - for example, a severity field may only be relevant if a finding is confirmed, or a causative agent field may constrain which reaction types are appropriate. Identify and model these dependencies explicitly so that templates can guide clinicians and validate data at entry, rather than relying on post-hoc correction.

decisions.question: What language reference set and display terms will be used for each clinical context?
decisions.guidance: Configure the terminology service to return preferred terms from the appropriate national language reference set. Terms displayed in templates must come from the language reference set - not FSNs or arbitrary synonyms. In multilingual deployments, agree language priority order and fallback behaviour explicitly. See the Search and data entry playbook for term display and synonym configuration guidance.

decisions.question: How will ongoing maintenance, quality assurance, and change management be handled?
decisions.guidance: Structured documentation must remain maintainable as clinical requirements evolve and SNOMED CT is updated. Establish processes that allow value sets and templates to be updated in response to both clinician requests and terminology releases - without requiring full system redevelopment. Track free-text rates, out-of-scope concept usage, and template completion as quality indicators. See the Governance playbook for release management process guidance.

steps.title: Define documentation requirements per clinical area
steps.description: Work with clinical leads to identify which fields require structured SNOMED CT coding, what granularity is needed, and how data will be used downstream. Prioritise fields that feed decision support, analytics, or cross-system exchange - these deliver the most value from structured coding.

steps.title: Determine context representation requirements
steps.description: For each structured field, decide whether clinical context needs to be captured alongside the coded value - for example, whether a finding is confirmed, suspected, or excluded. Consult the Context Representation Implementation Guide to identify the appropriate pattern. These decisions must be made before value set binding, as they affect which concepts are appropriate for each field and how downstream queries should be written.

steps.title: Define value set binding for each structured field
steps.description: Select the appropriate binding approach for each field. ECL is well-suited to hierarchy-based constraints that stay current with new SNOMED CT releases; curated reference sets suit fields where clinical judgement over individual concept inclusion is required. Package value sets as FHIR ValueSet resources for runtime use by the terminology service. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring and testing guidance.

options.label: ECL CONSTRAINT (INTENSIONAL)
points: Write an ECL expression that captures the intended concept scope from the SNOMED CT hierarchy
New concepts added in future SNOMED CT releases that satisfy the constraint are included automatically
Best for fields with a clear hierarchical scope - for example, all findings, all procedures, all substances
Requires a terminology service with ECL expansion support at runtime

example.label: ECL for a documentation field
example.code:
# All clinical findings (broad - appropriate for general finding fields)
<<404684003 |Clinical finding (finding)|

# Narrowed to disorders (common for diagnosis fields)
<<64572001 |Disease (disorder)|

# Causative agents for allergy/adverse reaction fields
<<105590001 |Substance (substance)| OR <<373873005 |Pharmaceutical / biologic product (product)|

# Severity qualifier (for severity fields)
<<272141005 |Severities (qualifier value)|

options.label: CURATED REFERENCE SET (EXTENSIONAL)
points: Select individual concepts based on clinical review and publish as an RF2 simple reference set or FHIR ValueSet with explicit entries
Gives clinical control over exactly which concepts appear - useful for fields where the hierarchy includes inappropriate concepts
Must be reviewed and updated on each SNOMED CT release to handle inactivated concepts and new clinical content
Best for small, highly curated pick-lists or fields where ECL cannot cleanly express the intended scope

steps.title: Establish logic and dependencies between data elements
steps.description: Identify fields that are clinically interdependent and implement the necessary logic in the template or data entry layer - conditional field display, cross-field validation, or guided value selection. Document these dependencies explicitly so they can be maintained as templates evolve.

steps.title: Implement data entry UX with correct term display and validation
steps.description: Build autocomplete and pick-list controls that query the terminology service and display preferred terms from the configured language reference set. Never surface FSNs in clinical-facing UI. Use $validate-code to confirm that a concept submitted by a client is active, from the correct edition, and within the field's value set. See the Search and data entry playbook for ranking, synonym configuration, and no-match handling.

examples.label: FHIR Observation with SNOMED CT code
$validate-code for field validation

steps.title: Establish maintenance, QA, and change management processes
steps.description: Define processes for updating value sets and templates in response to clinician requests and SNOMED CT releases. Ensure that changes can be made without full system redevelopment. Track quality indicators - free-text rates, out-of-scope concept usage, template completion - and establish governance for who approves changes and how updates are communicated to clinical teams. See the Governance playbook for release review process guidance.

dependencies.text: Terminology service supporting value set expansion ($expand) and code validation ($validate-code)
Value sets defined per documentation field, using ECL constraints or curated reference sets
Language reference set for preferred term display and synonym search
Clinical governance for field binding, context representation, and change management

pitfalls: Replacing free text entirely where supplementing it would be more appropriate - over-structuring creates clinician friction and workarounds
Not considering context representation - a coded value without context (confirmed vs. suspected, patient vs. family history) cannot be reliably queried or exchanged
Defaulting to ECL for all value set bindings - some fields are better served by curated reference sets where clinical judgement over individual concept inclusion is required
Displaying FSNs to clinicians in documentation templates - FSNs are technical identifiers, not display labels
Skipping $validate-code on received or submitted concept IDs - invalid or out-of-scope codes silently enter the clinical record
No change management process - structured documentation becomes a maintenance burden when clinician requirements evolve or SNOMED CT releases inactivate concepts used in existing records

cds.title: Clinical decision support
cds.subtitle: Using SNOMED CT hierarchies and ECL to power computable clinical rules
cds.overview:
SNOMED CT enables computable clinical logic through its hierarchical concept model and Expression Constraint Language (ECL).

Rules built on SNOMED CT subsumption - using ECL expressions such as <<73211009 for all descendants of Diabetes mellitus - automatically cover all clinically relevant child concepts, including those added in future SNOMED CT releases. This makes CDS rules significantly more durable and clinically complete than rules based on explicit flat code lists.

Effective CDS keeps two layers apart: references to clinical entities (conditions, findings, procedures, medications), which are represented with SNOMED CT, and the decision logic that combines them (conditions, thresholds, timing, actions), which is expressed in the formalism of the CDS engine. The two layers meet where the logic references SNOMED CT value sets or ECL expressions.

decisions.question: What clinical logic needs to be expressed as computable rules?
decisions.guidance: Document each rule in plain clinical language before attempting SNOMED CT representation. Alerts, reminders, order sets, contraindication checks, and care pathway triggers all have different implementation patterns. Clarify which rules are mandatory vs. advisory, and what evidence base supports them.

decisions.question: What formalism will express the decision logic?
decisions.guidance: The formalism is usually dictated by the CDS engine: decision tables (e.g., DMN) for rules maintained by clinical or business analysts, simple logical expressions (JSON rules, FHIRPath) for lightweight engines, CQL with FHIR Clinical Reasoning resources (Library, PlanDefinition) for shareable, standards-based knowledge artifacts, or a general-purpose programming language when logic lives in application code. Consider who will author and maintain the rules, portability across systems, and testability. Whatever the choice, the formalism must reference SNOMED CT through value sets or ECL rather than embedding code lists. See step 6 for a comparison of the options.

decisions.question: Will rule elements use ECL subsumption queries or explicit concept lists?
decisions.guidance: ECL subsumption (e.g., <<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus|) is strongly preferred - it automatically includes all subtypes and survives concept additions in new SNOMED CT releases. Explicit concept lists must be manually updated on each release, creating maintenance burden and coverage gaps. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring guidance.

decisions.question: How will SNOMED CT-coded data be queried at runtime?
decisions.guidance: Clarify whether your CDS engine will call the terminology service API at the point of firing (real-time subsumption check) or use pre-expanded concept sets stored locally. Real-time calls via the terminology service are accurate and always reflect the current SNOMED CT release; pre-expanded sets are faster but require refresh on each release. See step 7 for a detailed comparison of both approaches.

decisions.question: What data quality requirements must be met before CDS is reliable?
decisions.guidance: CDS is only as good as the coded data it queries. Clarify the minimum coding completeness, concept specificity, and recency required before CDS rules will produce meaningful results. Poor data quality can trigger false positives and clinician alert fatigue. Consult the Analytics playbook for query patterns that assess data quality before deploying rules.

decisions.question: How will clinical rules be governed, approved, and retired?
decisions.guidance: Establish a clinical rule lifecycle process before go-live. Rules must be approved by clinical leads, tested against real patient data, versioned, and retired when clinical evidence changes. Governance is as important as the technical implementation.

steps.title: Document each rule in plain clinical language
steps.description: Write each rule as a clinical statement - who it applies to, what it checks, and what action it triggers. This is the source of truth that the SNOMED CT representation must faithfully express. Include the clinical evidence base and the intended alert or action so that both clinical and technical reviewers can validate the final implementation.

steps.title: Separate clinical entity references from decision logic
steps.description: Decompose each rule into two kinds of element. Clinical entity references - diagnoses, findings, signs and symptoms, risk factors, procedures, medications, allergies - are what SNOMED CT represents; each becomes a rule element for steps 3 to 5. Decision logic - boolean combinations (AND, OR, NOT), numeric thresholds, age and demographic criteria, temporal windows, counts, and the resulting action - belongs to the formalism of the CDS engine (step 6). Some elements need another code system (laboratory tests are commonly LOINC-coded), and some depend on the information model rather than the terminology: whether a condition is active, confirmed, or recorded as family history is carried by the record structure (e.g., FHIR Condition.clinicalStatus, Condition.verificationStatus, FamilyMemberHistory), not by the SNOMED CT code. Keeping the layers separate lets terminology and logic be authored, versioned, and maintained independently.

examples.label: Rule decomposition
examples.code:
# Rule in plain clinical language (from step 1)
# "Alert when an adult with diabetes mellitus has an active NSAID
#  prescription and a most recent eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m2"

# Clinical entity references -> SNOMED CT (steps 3-5)
Diabetes mellitus    <<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus (disorder)|
NSAID products       < 763158003 |Medicinal product (product)| :
                         127489000 |Has active ingredient (attribute)| =
                         <<372665008 |Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent (substance)|

# Other code systems
eGFR test            LOINC value set (laboratory observation)

# Information model (record context, not terminology)
Condition active     Condition.clinicalStatus = active
Prescription active  MedicationRequest.status = active

# Decision logic -> CDS engine formalism (step 6)
age >= 18
AND has diabetes AND on NSAID
AND most recent eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2
THEN alert "Review NSAID use - diabetes with reduced eGFR"

steps.title: Map clinical entity references to SNOMED CT concepts
steps.description: For each clinical entity reference identified in step 2, find the most appropriate concept using an available browser or authoring tool. Prefer finding a single parent concept whose descendants cover all intended cases, enabling a clean ECL subsumption expression. Use the Browser's hierarchy view to verify that the descendant set is clinically appropriate before writing ECL.

steps.title: Write ECL expressions for each rule element
steps.description: Express each rule element as an ECL constraint. Use subsumption (<<) to capture entire disease or drug families. Combine constraints using set operators (AND, OR, MINUS) and attribute refinements for precision. Test expressions using the terminology service $expand operation to confirm the concept set is clinically complete. See the Value set playbook for ECL authoring guidance.

examples.label: ECL: condition subsumption
examples.code:
# All types of diabetes mellitus
<<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus (disorder)|

# All types of hypertension
<<38341003 |Hypertensive disorder, systemic arterial (disorder)|

# Cardiovascular disease excluding hypertension
<<49601007 |Disorder of cardiovascular system (disorder)| MINUS <<38341003 |Hypertensive disorder, systemic arterial (disorder)|

examples.label: ECL: medication subsumption
examples.code:
# All metformin products (by precise active ingredient)
<<372726002 |Metformin (substance)|

# All NSAIDs (by pharmacological class)
<<372665008 |Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent (substance)|

# Rule combining condition and medication
# (evaluate independently and join in CDS logic)
# Condition: <<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus|
# Medication: <<372665008 |NSAID|

examples.label: ECL: attribute-refined query
examples.code:
# Procedures with finding site = kidney structure
# (example of attribute-based refinement)
<<71388002 |Procedure (procedure)| : 363704007 |Procedure site - Direct| = <<64033007 |Kidney structure (body structure)|

# Expand to check the resulting concept set
GET /fhir/ValueSet/$expand
  ?url=http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/<<71388002%20:%20363704007%20=%20<<64033007
  &count=20

steps.title: Package ECL expressions as value sets for the CDS engine
steps.description: Publish each ECL expression as a versioned FHIR ValueSet resource with a canonical URL. The CDS engine references the value set by URL rather than embedding an inline ECL string, giving rules a stable, auditable concept set that can be updated independently. See the Value set playbook for packaging and versioning patterns.

examples.label: FHIR ValueSet for CDS rule element

steps.title: Express the decision logic in the engine's formalism
steps.description: Implement the decision logic identified in step 2 in the formalism chosen for the CDS engine. Whatever the formalism, the logic never contains enumerated code lists: it references SNOMED CT through a value set canonical URL (preferred - versioned and governed, see step 5) or an ECL expression, and delegates membership checks to the terminology service (step 7). The examples below express the same rule from step 2 in each formalism, so the only thing that changes is the logic syntax - the SNOMED CT references stay the same.

options.label: DECISION TABLES (DMN)
points: Rules expressed as rows of input conditions and outcomes - readable and maintainable by clinical and business analysts
Input columns test value set membership (by canonical URL) or an ECL constraint; the table itself holds only thresholds, combinations, and actions
Well suited to families of similar rules that vary by a few parameters; less suited to complex temporal logic

options.label: SIMPLE LOGICAL EXPRESSIONS
points: Boolean conditions written as JSON rules, FHIRPath, or an engine-specific expression syntax
Lightweight and easy to embed; membership operators (in value set, in ECL) delegate SNOMED CT checks to the terminology service
Limited expressiveness and portability - each engine has its own syntax

options.label: CQL + FHIR CLINICAL REASONING
points: HL7 Clinical Quality Language packaged in FHIR Library and PlanDefinition resources, typically delivered via CDS Hooks
Declares value sets by canonical URL, including implicit ECL value sets (http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/...)
Shareable, standards-based, and testable across systems; steeper learning curve and requires a CQL engine

options.label: GENERAL-PURPOSE LANGUAGE
points: Logic written directly in application code (Python, Java, etc.) or in a rules engine
Maximum flexibility and performance; call the terminology service for membership checks instead of hard-coding code lists
Logic is opaque to clinical reviewers and hard to share - trace each implementation back to its plain-language rule from step 1

examples.label: Decision table referencing SNOMED CT
examples.code:
# Each input tests membership in a SNOMED CT value set (canonical URL)
# or an ECL constraint; the table holds only the decision logic

Inputs:
  Diabetes = condition.code in VS https://example.org/ValueSet/diabetes-mellitus-cds
               (<<73211009 |Diabetes mellitus (disorder)|)
  NSAID    = medication.code in ECL
               < 763158003 |Medicinal product| : 127489000 |Has active ingredient| = << 372665008 |Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent|
  eGFR     = latest Observation in VS https://example.org/ValueSet/egfr-loinc

| Age  | Diabetes | NSAID | eGFR  | -> Action                     |
|------|----------|-------|-------|-------------------------------|
| >=18 | true     | true  | < 60  | ALERT: review NSAID use       |
| >=18 | true     | true  | >= 60 | INFO: monitor renal function  |
| -    | -        | -     | -     | no action                     |

examples.label: JSON rule referencing SNOMED CT
CQL referencing SNOMED CT
examples.code:
library DiabetesNsaidRenal version '1.0.0'
using FHIR version '4.0.1'
include FHIRHelpers version '4.0.1'

codesystem "ConditionClinical": 'http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/condition-clinical'
code "active": 'active' from "ConditionClinical"

// Versioned, governed value set (recommended)
valueset "Diabetes mellitus": 'https://example.org/ValueSet/diabetes-mellitus-cds'
// Implicit ECL value set (useful for prototyping); decoded ECL:
// < 763158003 : 127489000 = << 372665008
valueset "NSAID products": 'http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/%3C%20763158003%20%3A%20127489000%20%3D%20%3C%3C%20372665008'
valueset "eGFR tests": 'https://example.org/ValueSet/egfr-loinc'

context Patient

define "Has diabetes":
  exists [Condition: "Diabetes mellitus"] C
    where C.clinicalStatus ~ "active"

define "On NSAID":
  exists [MedicationRequest: "NSAID products"] M
    where M.status = 'active'

define "Low eGFR":
  (Last([Observation: "eGFR tests"] O sort by (effective as FHIR.dateTime)).value as Quantity)
    < 60 'mL/min/{1.73_m2}'

define "Fire alert":
  AgeInYears() >= 18 and "Has diabetes" and "On NSAID" and "Low eGFR"

examples.label: Python referencing SNOMED CT
examples.code:
DIABETES_VS = "https://example.org/ValueSet/diabetes-mellitus-cds"
NSAID_ECL = ("< 763158003 |Medicinal product| : 127489000 |Has active ingredient| = "
             "<< 372665008 |Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent|")

def fire_alert(patient, ts):  # ts = terminology service client
    # SNOMED CT: membership resolved by the terminology service, never hard-coded lists
    has_diabetes = any(ts.validate_code(DIABETES_VS, c.code)
                       for c in patient.active_conditions)
    on_nsaid = any(ts.in_ecl(NSAID_ECL, m.code)
                   for m in patient.active_medications)
    # Decision logic: demographics, thresholds, combination
    return (patient.age >= 18 and has_diabetes and on_nsaid
            and patient.latest_egfr < 60)

steps.title: Implement subsumption-based queries via the terminology service
steps.description: Configure the CDS engine to check whether a patient's coded data falls within a rule's SNOMED CT constraint. Use the FHIR $subsumes operation for concept-to-concept hierarchical checks, or $validate-code to confirm a patient concept is within a named value set. This is the standard FHIR Terminology Service pattern. See the Terminology service playbook for deployment and the Analytics playbook for subsumption-based query patterns against clinical data stores.

examples.label: FHIR $subsumes: hierarchical check
examples.code:
# Check whether concept A subsumes concept B
# (i.e., B is a subtype of A)
GET /fhir/CodeSystem/$subsumes
  ?system=http://snomed.info/sct
  &codeA=73211009
  &codeB=44054006

# Response: outcome = "subsumes" means codeA is an ancestor of codeB
# (44054006 |Type 2 diabetes mellitus| IS a subtype of 73211009 |Diabetes mellitus|)
{
  "resourceType": "Parameters",
  "parameter": [
    { "name": "outcome", "valueCode": "subsumes" }
  ]
}

# Possible outcome values:
#   subsumes      - codeA is a supertype of codeB
#   subsumed-by   - codeA is a subtype of codeB
#   equivalent    - identical meaning
#   not-subsumed  - no hierarchical relationship

examples.label: FHIR $validate-code: value set membership

options.label: REAL-TIME SUBSUMPTION CHECK
points: CDS engine calls the terminology service $subsumes or ECL $expand endpoint at the point of rule firing
Always reflects the current SNOMED CT release - new subtypes are automatically included
Adds latency to each rule evaluation - acceptable for most clinical workflows
Requires a reliable, low-latency connection to the terminology service

options.label: PRE-EXPANDED CONCEPT SETS
points: ECL expressions are expanded at load time and stored as flat concept ID sets in the CDS engine's local store
Fast evaluation with no runtime terminology service dependency
Must be refreshed on each SNOMED CT release - new subtypes are silently excluded until the next refresh
Suitable for high-frequency rules where latency is critical and a scheduled refresh process is in place

steps.title: Test, approve, and release each rule through governance
steps.description: Test rules against real patient data, validate results with clinical subject matter experts, and formally approve before go-live. Document the clinical evidence base, the SNOMED CT value sets used (with version), and the planned review schedule. Ensure that historical patient data coded with older SNOMED CT concept IDs is included in testing - inactivated concepts may silently fall outside a rule's value set.

dependencies.text: Terminology service with ECL, $subsumes, and $validate-code support
ECL-defined, versioned value sets for each rule element
Structured, SNOMED CT-coded clinical data of sufficient quality and completeness
Clinical governance process for rule approval, versioning, and retirement

pitfalls: Using explicit concept lists instead of ECL subsumption - new child concepts added in SNOMED CT releases silently fall outside the rule
Firing CDS rules against poorly coded or incomplete data - produces false positives that erode clinician trust
No rule governance - outdated alerts that contradict current evidence persist in production and create clinical risk
Testing only against current SNOMED CT content - historical patient data may use older, now-inactivated concept IDs that fall outside the ECL constraint
Skipping value set versioning - it becomes impossible to audit which concept set a historical rule used when fired
Pre-expanded concept sets without a refresh process - after each SNOMED CT release, new subtypes are silently excluded from rule evaluation

Mixing the terminology and logic layers - hard-coding SNOMED CT code lists inside rule logic (which then silently misses new subtypes), or pushing logic into the terminology layer (value sets that encode thresholds, timing, or combinations of conditions) - makes rules opaque to review and impossible to maintain independently

Relying on the SNOMED CT code alone for record context - a diabetes code recorded as family history, or as a refuted or resolved condition, fires the rule unless the information model's status and context fields are also checked

analytics.title: Analytics and reporting
analytics.subtitle: Using SNOMED CT subsumption, defining relationships, reference sets and maps to retrieve, aggregate and report clinical data
analytics.overview:
The main benefit of recording clinical data with SNOMED CT comes when that data is retrieved, analysed and reused - for point of care summaries and reporting, for population-based analysis such as trend analysis, clinical audit and pharmacovigilance, and for clinical research such as identifying trial candidates.

SNOMED CT supports this in ways a flat code list cannot: subsumption groups detailed concepts into broader categories at any level of detail, defining relationships let queries select concepts by their meaning (finding site, morphology, causative agent), reference sets capture curated groupings that the hierarchy does not express, and maps bring data coded in other code systems into SNOMED CT, or take SNOMED CT data out to classifications such as ICD-10 for statistical reporting.

Expression Constraint Language (ECL) is the standard way to express the terminology part of a query, but SNOMED CT does not dictate a query language or data architecture: the terminology logic is embedded in, or joined to, the query over the patient records.

Reliable results depend on more than the terminology. A SNOMED CT code alone does not say whether a condition is confirmed, suspected, or a family history - that context may sit in the information model. Longitudinal data contains concepts that have since been inactivated, and SNOMED CT's polyhierarchy means one concept can be counted in more than one category. This playbook covers how to define analytic categories, execute them against patient data, and handle context, versioning and aggregation correctly.

decisions.question: What analytic task needs to be supported, and what does it require of the data?
decisions.guidance: Point of care analytics (historical summaries, patient-level reporting), population-based analytics (trend analysis, surveillance, clinical audit, service planning) and clinical research (trial candidate identification, predictive medicine) have different requirements for precision, recall, timeliness and output format. Agree the clinical question, the population, the time period, the data sources and the required output before writing any query. A question that needs exact counts in mutually exclusive categories leads to different design choices than one that needs every potentially relevant patient for manual review.

decisions.question: Is all the source data coded with SNOMED CT?
decisions.guidance: Records often combine native SNOMED CT data with legacy or local codes, other code systems, and free text. Data coded in another code system can be brought into SNOMED CT analytics through a map, but the direction and correlation of the map matter: the map must go from the source codes to SNOMED CT, and use cases where safety or accuracy matters need exact-match maps. Free text can be encoded using natural language processing. Decide which sources are in scope and how each will be prepared - see the Mapping playbook and the Migration playbook.

decisions.question: Where is the clinical context of each code recorded?
decisions.guidance: A diagnosis of 56265001 |Heart disease| does not mean the patient has heart disease: it may be suspected, refuted, or a family history. Context can be carried by the information model (a section heading, a status or verification element), precoordinated in the concept (394886001 |Heart disease suspected|), or recorded in a separate coded element. Find out how each source system records context before designing queries, and agree rules for combining it - especially for negation, where the information model and the terminology can both say 'absent'.

decisions.question: How will each analytic category be defined?
decisions.guidance: Use subsumption (<<) where a single concept and its subtypes match the category, defining relationships (attribute refinements) where the category is defined by a characteristic such as finding site or causative agent, and a reference set where the category is a curated grouping the hierarchy does not express (for example, rare diseases). These techniques can be combined in one ECL expression. Avoid lexical (text-matching) queries for defining categories - use them only to find candidates for review. See the Value set design and management playbook for authoring guidance.

decisions.question: How will the terminology part of the query be executed against patient data?
decisions.guidance: Record queries (SQL, AQL, SPARQL, or an analytics tool) must be combined with terminology queries. The main options are calling a terminology service that evaluates ECL at query time, joining to a transitive closure table loaded into the data platform, or using concept sets or reference sets expanded in advance. Choose based on the data architecture (querying operational records, a data warehouse, or distributed storage), query volume, and whether results must reflect the latest release or a fixed version. See step 5 for a comparison.

decisions.question: How will data recorded against older SNOMED CT releases be included?
decisions.guidance: Longitudinal records keep the concepts that were active when the data was recorded, so their share of inactive concepts grows over time. A standard ECL query returns only active concepts and silently misses these records. Decide, per use case, how much historical content to include using historical association reference sets: high precision for decision support, a balance of precision and recall for research and audit, and maximum recall for identifying records for manual review.

decisions.question: Are mutually exclusive categories or classification codes required in the output?
decisions.guidance: SNOMED CT is a polyhierarchy: 154283005 |Pulmonary tuberculosis| is both a respiratory disorder and an infectious disease, so subsumption-based categories can overlap. That suits clinical questions, but statistical returns, epidemiological counts and reimbursement need each case counted once. Where that is needed, or where the output must be in ICD-10 or another classification, use a published map such as the SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map - see the Mapping playbook.

steps.title: Define the analytic question and decompose it into categories
steps.description: Write the question in plain clinical language - who is counted, over what period, from which data sources, and what output is needed. Then separate the clinical categories that SNOMED CT will define (conditions, procedures, medications, findings) from the record logic that the query language handles (dates, counts, demographics, status, care setting). Each clinical category becomes a terminology definition in step 4; the record logic stays in the record query. Keeping the two apart lets terminology definitions be reused, reviewed and versioned independently of the reports that use them.

examples.label: Question decomposition
examples.code:
# Analytic question in plain clinical language
# "Number of adults with diabetes mellitus and a recorded kidney
#  disease, per year, 2020-2025, from primary care records"

# Clinical categories -> SNOMED CT definitions (step 4)
Diabetes mellitus   << 73211009 |Diabetes mellitus (disorder)|
Kidney disease      << 90708001 |Kidney disease (disorder)|

# Record context -> information model (step 3)
Condition is about the patient, confirmed, not refuted

# Record logic -> record query language (step 5)
age >= 18 at date of record
recorded between 2020-01-01 and 2025-12-31
count distinct patients, grouped by year

steps.title: Prepare the data for SNOMED CT analytics
steps.description: Assess which data is natively coded with SNOMED CT and which is not. Bring data from other code systems into SNOMED CT using maps that go from the source code system to SNOMED CT; maps built for the opposite direction serve poorly in reverse unless every link is an exact match. Where accuracy matters (data integration, decision support), use exact-match maps; for epidemiology or service planning, mapping to a broader SNOMED CT concept may be acceptable but should be documented. In a data warehouse, this preparation happens in the staging layer of the extract, transform and load process. Keep the original source code alongside the mapped concept so that the transformation can be audited, and check that no meaning is lost along the way. See the Mapping playbook for map design and the Migration playbook for moving legacy data.

steps.title: Resolve record context alongside the code
steps.description: Identify every way the source systems record context for the categories in scope - section headings such as 'Family history', status and verification elements (for example FHIR Condition.clinicalStatus and Condition.verificationStatus), separate coded elements such as 'diagnosis type', and context precoordinated in SNOMED CT concepts below 413350009 |Finding with explicit context|. The same meaning may be recorded differently across systems, or even across users of the same system. Write the query so that it reads both the code and its context, and harmonise the representations when integrating data from several sources. Without this step, family history, suspected and refuted entries are counted as confirmed patient conditions.

examples.label: Two ways of recording family history
examples.code:
# System A: context in the information model
Section: "Family history"
Problem: 56265001 |Heart disease (disorder)|

# System B: context precoordinated in the concept
Problem: 275120007 |Family history of cardiac disorder (situation)|

# A query for patients' own heart disease must exclude both.
# A query for family history of heart disease must find both:
#   - entries in the family history section with code in << 56265001
#   - entries with code in
<< 416471007 |Family history of clinical finding (situation)| :
  246090004 |Associated finding| = << 56265001 |Heart disease (disorder)|

steps.title: Define each category using SNOMED CT techniques
steps.description: Express each clinical category from step 1 as a terminology definition, preferably in ECL. Choose the technique that matches how the category is defined, and combine techniques where needed. Validate each definition by expanding it with a terminology service: check the count and review the members with clinical experts before running it against patient data. Package definitions that will be reused as versioned value sets or reference sets - see the Value set design and management playbook.

options.label: SUBSUMPTION
points: Selects a concept and all its subtypes using << (descendant or self) or < (descendant)
The fundamental SNOMED CT analytic technique: 'any kind of infectious disease' finds viral pneumonia, tuberculosis and every other subtype
New subtypes added in future releases are included automatically
Use when one concept in the hierarchy matches the meaning of the category

example.label: ECL: subsumption
example.code:
# Any kind of infectious disease
<< 40733004 |Infectious disease (disorder)|

# Any kind of diabetes mellitus
<< 73211009 |Diabetes mellitus (disorder)|

options.label: DEFINING RELATIONSHIPS
points: Selects concepts by the value of their defining attributes, such as finding site, associated morphology or causative agent
Answers questions the hierarchy alone does not, such as 'all benign neoplasms of the kidney'
Use subsumption on the attribute value (<<) so that more specific values are also matched
Also matches postcoordinated data that is not a subtype of any single precoordinated concept

example.label: ECL: attribute refinement
example.code:
# Benign neoplasms of the kidney
< 404684003 |Clinical finding (finding)| :
  116676008 |Associated morphology| = << 3898006 |Neoplasm, benign (morphologic abnormality)| ,
  363698007 |Finding site| = << 64033007 |Kidney structure (body structure)|

# Disorders caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex in the lung
< 64572001 |Disease (disorder)| :
  246075003 |Causative agent| = << 113858008 |Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (organism)| ,
  363698007 |Finding site| = << 39607008 |Lung structure (body structure)|

options.label: SUBSETS AND REFERENCE SETS
points: Selects concepts by membership of a curated subset, distributed and versioned as a reference set
Use for groupings the hierarchy does not express, such as rare diseases or a national reporting list
Referenced in ECL with ^ (memberOf); combine with subsumption to include subtypes of members
Extensional subsets need manual review on each release; prefer an ECL definition where the category can be expressed that way

example.label: ECL: reference set membership
example.code:
# Members of a reference set (example identifier)
^ 649999999104 |Example rare disease simple reference set|

# Members of the reference set and all their subtypes
<< (^ 649999999104 |Example rare disease simple reference set|)

steps.title: Execute the terminology logic within the record query
steps.description: Combine each terminology definition with the record logic from step 1. Avoid pasting long lists of concept identifiers into queries - they are hard to validate and maintain, and can exceed query engine limits. Choose an execution approach that fits the data architecture: analytics directly over operational records, over a data warehouse, or over distributed storage. Whichever approach is used, pin the SNOMED CT edition and version so that results can be reproduced.

options.label: LIVE ECL VIA TERMINOLOGY SERVICE
points: The analytics platform passes ECL to the terminology service ($expand) at query time, or the query language supports ECL directly
Supports the full range of ECL, including attribute refinements, reference set membership and history supplements
Always reflects the configured release; pin the version when results must be reproducible
Best for interactive and ad hoc analysis; requires a reliable connection from the analytics environment

example.label: FHIR $expand with version pinned
example.code:
GET /fhir/ValueSet/$expand
  ?url=http://snomed.info/sct?fhir_vs=ecl/<< 73211009
  &system-version=http://snomed.info/sct|http://snomed.info/sct/900000000000207008/version/20251101
  &count=100

# Use expansion.total to sense-check scope before running against patient data

options.label: TRANSITIVE CLOSURE TABLE
points: A table holding every subtype-supertype pair, generated from the snapshot relationships file and loaded into the data platform
Subsumption becomes a simple, fast join - well suited to a data warehouse and large batch queries
Covers subsumption only; attribute refinements and reference set membership need the relationship and reference set tables as well
Must be regenerated on each SNOMED CT release

example.label: SQL with a transitive closure table
example.code:
-- Patients with any kind of respiratory system disorder
SELECT DISTINCT pl.patient_id
FROM problem_list pl
JOIN snomed_transitive_closure tc
  ON tc.subtype_id = pl.concept_id
WHERE tc.supertype_id = 50043002  -- |Disorder of respiratory system|
  AND pl.verification_status = 'confirmed'

UNION

-- include the category concept itself (<< is descendant OR self)
SELECT DISTINCT patient_id FROM problem_list
WHERE concept_id = 50043002 AND verification_status = 'confirmed'

options.label: PRE-EXPANDED CONCEPT SETS
points: Each ECL definition is expanded in advance and stored as a table or reference set that queries join to
Fast, with no runtime terminology dependency, and supports any ECL the expansion tool supports
Must be re-expanded on each SNOMED CT release - new subtypes are silently excluded until then
Record the ECL, edition, version and expansion date with each set so that results can be audited

example.label: SQL with a pre-expanded concept set
example.code:
-- concept_set_member is populated by expanding
-- << 73211009 |Diabetes mellitus| against edition 20251101
SELECT DISTINCT c.patient_id
FROM condition c
JOIN concept_set_member m
  ON m.concept_id = c.concept_id
WHERE m.set_id = 'diabetes-mellitus'
  AND m.set_version = '20251101'
  AND c.clinical_status = 'active'

steps.title: Include inactive concepts using historical associations
steps.description: Clinical records keep the concepts that were active when the data was recorded, so a query run against the current release misses records coded with concepts that have since been inactivated. Rather than running the query against an old release, run it against the most recent release - whose definitions are generally the most accurate - and supplement the results with inactive concepts linked to the result set through historical association reference sets. ECL history supplements do this directly, with three profiles that trade precision against recall. Where the terminology service or data platform does not support history supplements, join to the historical association reference sets in the same way. See the Governance playbook for managing the impact of each new release.

examples.label: ECL history supplements

steps.title: Aggregate results and produce classification output where required
steps.description: When results are grouped into categories using subsumption, remember that SNOMED CT is a polyhierarchy: a patient with pulmonary tuberculosis is correctly counted under both respiratory disorders and infectious diseases. Make this explicit in reports, and do not add up overlapping categories as if they were exclusive. Where mutually exclusive categories, statistical returns or reimbursement codes are required, record the data in SNOMED CT and map it to the classification using a published map. The SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map is not a simple lookup: map groups, priorities, rules (which may test age, sex or other recorded conditions) and advice must be applied, and some concepts cannot be classified without further information. See the Mapping playbook for map application.

examples.label: Overlapping categories in a polyhierarchy
examples.code:
# 154283005 |Pulmonary tuberculosis| is a member of all three:
<< 50043002 |Disorder of respiratory system (disorder)|
<< 56717001 |Tuberculosis (disorder)|
<< 40733004 |Infectious disease (disorder)|

# Counts per category are correct individually,
# but the categories overlap and must not be summed.

examples.label: SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map rules
examples.code:
# 447562003 |SNOMED CT to ICD-10 extended map|
# Source concept: 15296000 |Sterility (finding)|

Group Priority Rule                                     Target
1     1        IFA 10114008 |Female sterility (finding)|  N97.9
1     2        IFA 49408009 |Male sterility (finding)|    N46
1     3        OTHERWISE TRUE                            (none)
               advice: MAP SOURCE CONCEPT CANNOT BE CLASSIFIED
                       WITH AVAILABLE DATA

# Evaluate rules in priority order within each group and take the
# first rule that is true. Each group contributes at most one target.

steps.title: Validate, version and govern queries and reports
steps.description: Review each terminology definition and its expansion with clinical experts before use, and test the full query against known patient records. Look out for results that are logically correct but clinically unexpected - SNOMED CT hierarchies follow formal definitions, so, for example, an insect bite of the nose is a kind of head injury. Where data may contain postcoordinated expressions, prefer attribute-based definitions, which also match expressions that are not subtypes of a single precoordinated concept. Record the ECL or reference set, the SNOMED CT edition and version, the history profile and any map used for each published result, and re-run validation on each new release. See the Governance playbook for review and change management.

dependencies.text: Terminology service with ECL support, reference set membership and a selectable edition and version - see the Terminology service playbook
Clinical data store holding SNOMED CT concept identifiers together with their record context (status, verification, section)
Validated, versioned ECL definitions, value sets or reference sets for each analytic category
Maps from source code systems to SNOMED CT, and from SNOMED CT to classifications where required
Governance process for query review, versioning and release management

pitfalls: Querying exact concept identifiers only - misses every subtype and produces systematically incomplete results
Ignoring record context - family history, suspected and refuted entries are counted as confirmed patient conditions
Querying the current release without historical associations - records coded with now-inactive concepts are silently excluded
Defining categories with text matching - lexical queries both miss relevant concepts and include irrelevant ones
Summing overlapping subsumption-based categories - SNOMED CT's polyhierarchy places one concept in several categories, so totals are double counted
Treating the ICD-10 map as a simple lookup - map rules, priorities and advice must be applied, or the wrong classification codes are produced
Using a map in the reverse direction to the one it was built for, or treating narrow-to-broad maps as exact - meaning shifts silently during data preparation
Pre-expanded concept sets or transitive closure tables without a refresh process - after each release, new subtypes are silently excluded
Not recording the edition, version and definition used - results cannot be reproduced or audited
